grandparents.lede: Born in a farm house at Buckhorn, Oklahoma, Bob jumped out of airplanes for the U.S. Army for twenty years and came home to Choctaw County.
A Grayson County farm girl who met Bob at a skating rink, married him in 1961, raised three children on Army posts around the world, and worked forty years as a respiratory therapist.
A Winona carpenter's son who married at twenty in front of 350 guests, raised five children along the Mississippi, and was killed on a La Crosse highway at thirty-eight.
The Rollingstone insurance agent's daughter who was widowed twice in two years, kept five children together, and worked at a La Crosse nursing home until the cancer that killed her at forty-seven.

stories.title: Twenty years and countless jumps
stories.hook: Bob Johnson left the Oklahoma farm country, became a paratrooper, served in Vietnam and twice in Korea, and retired a Warrant Officer 3.
body: In the 1950 census, a twelve-year-old named Bob is listed in a farmhouse on the road east of Sunkist, near Hunter in Choctaw County, Oklahoma. His father Joe is farming. His father's wife, Opal, is there, with a stepbrother, Don, and two small half-sisters. Bob's own mother, Nettie, had remarried and lived elsewhere. It was a crowded, working household in a county where most families still lived off cotton, corn and cattle.

Bobby Joe Johnson was born on 17 July 1937 at Buckhorn, a farming community in southeastern Oklahoma. His obituary says he spent most of his youth "in the rural area of Southeast Oklahoma, a place that he loved dearly." By his teens he was in Texas: the Army's hometown releases of 1958 and 1961 say he graduated from Decatur High School in 1957 and attended Decatur Baptist College. His obituary, written decades later, says Savoy, which is where his mother Nettie ended up and is buried. Somewhere in those years he met Marjorie Bell at a skating rink. She was six years younger.

The Army took him in February 1958. He finished basic training at Fort Ord, California, and that August the Hugo Daily News ran a front-page item, "Boswell GI Gets Paratroop Wings": Pvt. Bobby J. Johnson, son of Joel G. Johnson of the Boehler Route, had graduated from the 82d Airborne Division Jump School at Fort Bragg, North Carolina, after a course that included five training jumps. Paratroopers of that era trained at Fort Bragg and at Fort Campbell, Kentucky, which ran an Airborne Course from 1950 to 1962 and became home to the reactivated 101st Airborne Division in 1956.

By January 1961 he was a Specialist Four and a supply clerk in the Mortar Battery of the 82nd Airborne's 504th Infantry, last stationed in Germany. The Durant Daily Democrat reported that he took part with the 504th in President Kennedy's inaugural parade in Washington. The same item gives his mother's new name, Mrs. Nettie B. Tillery of Sadler, Texas; in 1958 the paper had called her Mrs. McCarter. Eleven months after the parade he married Margie. In July 1964 their son David was born in Christian County, Kentucky, the Fort Campbell area, so Bob was probably serving near there then; no record names his unit. His obituary sums up the rest: one tour in Vietnam, two in Korea, and postings across the United States, none of them dated. Korea in the late 1960s was not quiet. From 1966 to 1969 North Korean raiders clashed with American and South Korean troops along the DMZ, and after the January 1968 Blue House raid and the capture of the USS Pueblo the defenses there were stepped up. Bob's own tours may have fallen before, during or after that stretch.

After "twenty years and countless jumps," he retired as a Warrant Officer 3 and returned to Oklahoma. A warrant officer is a technical specialist, usually promoted from the enlisted ranks after years of experience, a long way from the Buckhorn farm boy who left for the Army. In retirement he read military biographies, watched westerns, and kept his yard and vehicles immaculate. His family remembered the uniform of civilian life: button-up shirts rolled to the elbows, starched jeans, cowboy boots and one of his many Airborne hats. A daily request to Margie was whether they could go and get the grandkids.

He and Margie raised three children, Joey, David and Leatha. David was killed on a highway in October 1988, at twenty-four. Bob died on 28 September 2024, aged eighty-seven, and was buried at Restland Cemetery in Boswell near his father Joe, who had served in the Army Air Forces' engineers in World War II. Two generations of Johnson men in uniform, both ending up in the same Choctaw County cemetery.

stories.title: Forty years of helping people breathe
stories.hook: Margie Bell met Bob Johnson at a Texas skating rink, followed his Army career for twenty years, then spent four decades at the bedside of patients who could not catch their breath.
body: In the spring of 1950 a census taker stopped at a farm in Grayson County, Texas, and wrote down seven-year-old Marjorie Bell with her parents, Wayne and Melba, and her brothers and sisters. It was an ordinary page for an ordinary farm family. Nothing on it suggests that the second-grader would one day cross the Atlantic and the Pacific on an Army wife's orders.

Marjorie Ann Bell was born on 16 March 1943 and grew up with her sisters Sylvia "Sue" and June and her brother Glenn, called Sonny. She played basketball and loved to skate. Her obituary says it was on one of those nights at the skating rink, in her teens, that she met Bobby Johnson, a farm boy from Choctaw County, Oklahoma, who was six years older and, by then, a paratrooper in the 82nd Airborne. She graduated from S&S Consolidated High School in 1961 and started college to study nursing. That January he had marched with the 504th Infantry in President Kennedy's inaugural parade. On 21 December 1961 she set the books aside and married him.

Bob was headed into an Army career, and Margie went with him. Their three children, Joey, David and Leatha, were born in the years that followed, David in 1964 at Christian County, Kentucky, the county that holds Fort Campbell. Her obituary says the family moved "more often than most," and that wherever they landed she worked to make the house a home. Twenty years of Army life meant packing boxes more times than most civilians ever will, and doing much of it while the soldier was somewhere else.

Her own career came out of that same roving life. She finished her schooling as a respiratory therapist and worked in the field for forty years, and she worked as an EMT as well. The obituary does not say where she trained or when. The trade she joined had begun as the job of "oxygen technicians," who in the 1930s and 1940s mostly hauled gas cylinders to hospital rooms and set up oxygen tents and nasal catheters, often trained on the job. By the time Margie entered it, it had become a licensed profession built around ventilators, breathing treatments and critically ill patients. She cared for people, her obituary says, "with a smile on her face."

After Bob retired they came home to southeastern Oklahoma. Her obituary remembers a woman who never opened a cookbook but whose homemade ice cream, German chocolate cake, fried chicken and pot roast were the family's standing requests; nobody left without leftovers. Her flower beds were good enough for a magazine cover, and she told them they "need a good drink" as she watered. She sang hymns, loved church, and always had a piece of Extra gum to hand out.

Her life had two hard losses. In October 1988 her son David, twenty-four, died after a pickup rolled on an Atoka County highway. On the other side of Rachel's family, David Nelton had died in a head-on crash in La Crosse, Wisconsin, in 1977, so a son lost on a highway was something both families knew. Then in September 2024 Bob died after sixty-two years of marriage. Margie followed him on 12 February 2025 at Calera, Oklahoma, aged eighty-one. Her memorial service was held at First Baptist Church in Boswell. Like her mother Melba before her, who raised four children and buried a baby on a Grayson County farm, she held a family together through the worst of it.

stories.title: 96 miles an hour on Highway 3
stories.hook: David Johnson, Bob and Margie's middle child, was a passenger in a pickup clocked at 96 mph east of Atoka on a Wednesday night in October 1988. He was twenty-four.
body: At about 7:35 on the evening of Wednesday, 19 October 1988, an Oklahoma Highway Patrol lieutenant was driving east on Highway 3, seven miles east of Atoka, when he clocked an oncoming 1980 Chevrolet pickup at 96 miles an hour. By the time he turned around the driver had lost control on a curve. The pickup rolled at least five times and came to rest on its side beside a fence line. The paper noted that the rear bumper seemed to have caught a tree, spinning the truck and tearing the tires off the rims. Both men inside had been thrown out: the driver, twenty-one, of Bennington, and his passenger, David Johnson of Boswell.

The Lane First Responders and two ambulances took them to Atoka Memorial Hospital. David was moved on to Texoma Medical Center in Denison, Texas, where he died at about 3 a.m. on Thursday, 20 October, of head and internal injuries. He was twenty-four. The trooper said alcohol was involved and that neither man wore a seat belt. The driver was charged with manslaughter on Friday.

David Glenn Johnson had been born on 8 July 1964 in Christian County, Kentucky, the county that holds Fort Campbell, while his father Bob was a career paratrooper. He was the middle child between Joey and Leatha. He grew up in the Army's moves and then in Boswell, and the school portraits in the family's collection show a long-haired boy in the class pictures, a basketball player in number 21, and a ballplayer at the plate.

The Atoka County Times ran the story on 26 October under a plain headline, "Boswell Man Killed in One-Vehicle Accident." It was the kind of item rural Oklahoma papers printed every few weeks in those years: a county highway, a curve, a hospital run, a charge. David was buried at Restland Cemetery in Boswell, where Bob's father Joe had been laid to rest sixteen years before.

The loss ran through both sides of Rachel's family. David Nelton had died in 1977 in a head-on crash in La Crosse, Wisconsin, at thirty-eight, and his widow Diane held the household together. Margie held hers together too. When Bob died thirty-six years later, his obituary listed David first among those who had gone before him.

stories.title: Joe Johnson of the Boehler route
stories.hook: A Soper-born stockman who built airfields in World War II and married two Tyson sisters, one after the other.
body: On 16 October 1940, a few weeks before the first peacetime draft numbers were drawn, Joel Gilbert Johnson filled out his registration card at Boehler, Oklahoma. He was thirty-two, self-employed, five feet eight, 180 pounds, with a ruddy complexion, black hair and brown eyes. For the person who would always know where to find him he gave his father, Joel.

Everyone called him Joe. He had been born at Soper in Choctaw County on 24 July 1908, the year after Oklahoma became a state, to Joel A. Johnson and Winnie Bozarth. Soper itself was barely six. It had sprung up in 1902 when the Arkansas and Choctaw Railway ran a line through southern Choctaw County, and it was named for the railroad's attorney. Joe grew up in the cotton, corn and cattle economy of that railroad country, and by 1930, at twenty-one, he was living at home in Boswell. His father was buying stock for a living.

Joe married Nettie Beatrice Tyson, and their son Bobby was born in 1937. In April 1940 the census taker found Nettie, twenty-six, and "Bobbin J.," two, at her father Albert Tyson's rented farm at Oakes, while Joe was at Boehler with his own father. The marriage did not last. Nettie later married Bob Tillery. By 1950 Joe was farming on the road east of Sunkist, near Hunter, and his wife was Opal, Nettie's younger sister, whose first husband had been a Wilson. Bob lived with them. Their story is told in the sisters' own.

The war interrupted. Joe enlisted on 25 May 1942, at thirty-three, and served until 21 October 1945 as a Technician Fifth Grade in the 872nd Engineer Aviation Battalion. Engineer aviation battalions were built to build airfields: each was organized to put in an advanced airdrome on its own, with runways, taxiways and the roads and buildings around them. The Army fielded 157 of them, and by war's end aviation engineers had built or improved more than a thousand airfields around the world. His record does not say where the 872nd worked, and this account does not guess.

Joe came home to the Boehler route and the cattle. When he died, early on Saturday, 25 November 1972, "after an apparent heart attack," the Paris News called him a World War II veteran, a member of the American Legion at Boswell and "a former stockman." The funeral was held at the Church of Christ in Boswell, and he was buried at Restland Cemetery, where the government headstone records his war service. His son Bob, who had spent his own career in Army airborne units, was by then in his thirties and a career soldier. Sixteen years later Restland took Joe's grandson David as well.

stories.title: Two sisters under one roof in 1940
stories.hook: In April 1940 the census taker found Nettie and Opal Tyson, both young mothers, back at their father's farm at Oakes. Ten years later Opal was married to Nettie's former husband.
body: That April the enumerator called at the rented farm of Albert Tyson at Oakes, in Choctaw County. Albert was sixty-five, born in Texas, schooled through the third grade, and farming on his own account. With him were his wife Elizabeth, fifty-nine, and their son Marion, seventeen. Also in the house were two grown daughters and their babies: Nettie Johnson, twenty-six, with her two-year-old son, written down as "Bobbin J. Johnson"; and Opal Wilson, twenty-one, with an infant son, Don.

The county was cotton, corn and hay country in the Depression years. Two married daughters and two grandchildren back under the parents' roof was not unusual, and the census does not say why. It shows that Nettie's husband Joe Johnson was not in the house, because his draft card that October puts him at Boehler with his own father. Opal's license is a matter of newspaper record: the Paris News of 12 July 1938 listed it among the Choctaw County marriage licenses, "Seidel Wilson to Opal Tyson, Boswell." She was eighteen.

A decade later the household had rearranged itself. In 1950 Joe Johnson was farming on the road east of Sunkist, near Hunter, with Opal as his wife. In the house were Bob, twelve, Opal's son Don, ten, listed as Joe's stepson, and two little daughters. The Arkansas marriage record in Sevier County shows Joel Gilbert Johnson, sixty, marrying Opal Wilson on 3 December 1968, and his obituary calls her "the former Opal Tyson." Nettie, meanwhile, married Bob Tillery, and their son Y. Q. Tillery, born at Boswell in 1942, became Bob's half-brother.

This is why the sources disagree about Bob's mother. Rachel's Ancestry tree attaches Opal to him, but the records made at the time point to Nettie. Army hometown releases name his mother as Mrs. Nettie B. McCarter of Sherman in 1958 and Mrs. Nettie B. Tillery of Sadler, Texas, in 1961, and his obituary agrees: "Joel Gilbert Johnson and Nettie Beatrice (Tyson) Johnson." Nettie died on 6 February 1980 and is buried at Sunnyside Cemetery in Savoy, Texas, where she had last lived. Bob grew up with his aunt as his stepmother, and the cousins in the Johnson household were also his siblings: his obituary lists Y. Q. Tillery and Don Wilson as brothers and Kay Caldwell and Sue Jones as sisters.
Opal's marriage to Joe came after Nettie's, and the two sisters ended up raising the same boy between them. The records give only the outline. They do not say what the sisters, or Bob, thought of it.

stories.title: Seven hours on Route 1
stories.hook: Wayne and Melba Bell married at Van Alstyne in 1937 and farmed Grayson County for forty years. In April 1954 they buried a baby son who lived seven hours.
body: Wayne Douglas Bell and Melba Nena Williams were married at Van Alstyne, Texas, on 18 September 1937. He was twenty-three, born at Anna in Collin County on 18 April 1914, the son of Charles Hercules "Lee" Bell and Mary Alice Baker. She was nineteen, born at Van Alstyne on 13 March 1918, the daughter of Cleave and Willie (Parker) Williams. Both had grown up within a few miles of Mantua, the seminary town that had died when the railroad missed it in 1872, and of the two railroad towns that replaced it.

They married in the Depression, when farming in the Blackland country was shrinking. Collin County lost more than 1,200 farms between 1930 and 1940, and Grayson County nearly 900. In 1940 the Bells were renters on Worchester Road in Grayson County, with their first baby, a daughter. Wayne was twenty-six, five feet ten, 175 pounds, with brown hair and gray eyes; when he registered for the draft that October he was working for Kimble Farms Inc.

By 1950 the family had grown to four children: Sue, eleven; Margie, seven, Rachel's grandmother; Glenn, four; and Norma June, two. The census taker wrote the youngest two as "Scharffer," but Margie's obituary names them as Glenn "Sonny" and June. In 1954 the Bells were on Route 1 near Collinsville. On 9 April Melba gave birth prematurely at St. Vincent's Hospital in Sherman to a son. He lived seven hours. The death certificate, signed by Dr. H. L. Brown, gives the cause as pulmonary edema due to premature birth, and Wayne signed as informant. The baby was buried the next day in West Hill Cemetery, Sherman. Margie was eleven.

Wayne came from a large family. When one of his sisters died in 1968, the paper named four sisters and four brothers still living: Ora Bell Russell, Mrs. J. R. Chapman, Mrs. Cecil Field and Mrs. S. W. Turner, and Charlie of Van Alstyne, Wayne of Denison, Jack of Galesburg, Illinois, and Hardy of Anna.

Melba belonged to Cherry Mound Baptist Church. She died at home in Denison on 22 September 1981, aged sixty-three, and was buried at Van Alstyne. Wayne died on 22 July 1991. Their daughter Margie had met a young Oklahoman at a skating rink and gone off with him on Army orders. In the end she raised her own children as her mother had, through moves, losses and long marriage.

stories.title: Joel Anderson Johnson, cattle buyer
stories.hook: Born in Milam County, Texas, in 1875, he came to Choctaw County around 1900 and bought and sold cattle for sixty years.
body: Joel Anderson Johnson was born on 2 April 1875 in Milam County, Texas, the cotton and ranch country east of Austin. His father was born in Arkansas and his mother in Mississippi, according to his census returns. In 1896 he married Minnie or Winnie W. Bozarth in Texas.

By 1910 they were in Oakes township, Choctaw County, Oklahoma, with five children: Aletha, twelve, Porter, nine, George, six, Willie, four, and Joel, one, who was Rachel's great-grandfather Joe. Statehood had come only three years earlier.

In 1930 the family owned a house in Boswell and Joel, fifty-five, was a stock buyer for a cattle compress. Their son Joel Gilbert, twenty-one, was still at home, along with a granddaughter, Lila Smith. In 1940 Joel and Winnie were farming on the road to Sunkist in Hunter township.

He died on a Wednesday night in March 1961 at the Memorial Hospital in Hugo, aged eighty-five, "retired farmer and rancher" and a resident of the community for sixty years. He was a member of the Church of Christ and was buried in Restland Cemetery. His obituary names his wife Winnie, his sons G. F. Johnson of Soper and Joe G. Johnson of Boswell, a daughter, Mrs. Riley King of Sterling, Texas, two brothers, Carl in California and Arthur in Colorado, and three sisters: Penny Cole of Hugo, Nannie Harrison of Soper and Sally Smith of Byars, Texas.

stories.title: A reception for 350 on the Rivers lawn
stories.hook: On a July morning in 1958 an eighteen-year-old from a Luxembourg village married a Winona carpenter's son, and half of Rollingstone ended up on her father's lawn.
body: The Saturday began early. At 9:30 on the morning of 26 July 1958, Diane Rivers, eighteen, walked up the aisle of Holy Trinity Catholic Church in Rollingstone, Minnesota, to marry David Nelton, nineteen. The Rev. George Moudry performed the double-ring ceremony and celebrated the nuptial Mass, and the altars were banked with pink and white gladioli and lighted candles. Her father, Edward, gave her away.

The Winona Daily News, which printed the account on 15 August with a studio photograph, recorded the dress down to the neckline: Chantilly lace and tulle over bridal satin, a lace bodice, long sleeves, a sabrina neckline, a full floor-length skirt, and a veil of silk illusion falling from a lace cap. She carried a cascade of white roses and a double orchid. The pearl necklace and bracelet were David's gift.

Look at who stood up with them and the whole village appears. Her sister Mary Lynn was maid of honor. The organist was Miss Angela Rivers, Diane's uncle Paul Rivers ushered, and her cousins served the Mass. The groom's side is thinner in the account: Douglas Trainor of Winona was best man, and David's sister Sandra a bridesmaid. This was Rivers country. The church itself had been raised in 1869 from rough-cut limestone by Luxembourg farmers who, in the words of the National Register nomination, 'provided the labor and financial aid', and the same families were still filling its pews ninety years later.

After a wedding dinner in the Flamingo Room of the Hotel Winona, the party drove back up the valley to the Edward Rivers home, where 350 people were fed on the lawn. Edward sold insurance in Rollingstone and his wife Viola had lived there all her married life, so a crowd that size was most of the parish and a good part of a large family. The Riverses had run the village post office and carried its rural mail since the 1880s, and Viola's Frisch people had farmed nearby at Oak Ridge.

The two families came from different sides of the same county. The Riverses and Frisches were Luxembourg Catholics who had settled the hills west of Winona in the 1850s and 1860s. The Neltons were Germans in town: George Nelton, David's grandfather, was a Winona house carpenter who became a contractor, and David himself was a Winona Senior High graduate who had spent time at Winona State College and now worked for his father, Arthur, a carpenter. Diane had finished Holy Trinity High School and Winona Secretarial School. Winona was a lumber, river and railroad city whose population had long been a mix of German, Polish and Yankee families, and weddings like this one stitched the town to the villages above it.

After a trip to the Wisconsin Dells the newlyweds were to be at home in Minnesota City, the small river settlement platted in 1852 where David's parents lived. The marriage lasted nineteen years, until a night in February 1977 that is told in the next story.

stories.title: Highway 53, 2:44 a.m.
stories.hook: At 2:44 on a February morning in 1977 a car and a pickup met head-on in La Crosse; David Nelton, a father of five, died half an hour later at thirty-eight.
body: The Winona Daily News gave the time to the minute. At 2:44 a.m. on Saturday 12 February 1977, David Nelton was driving north on Highway 53 near the George Street intersection in La Crosse, Wisconsin, when his car and a southbound pickup truck collided head-on in the south lane. He was taken to Lutheran Hospital and died there at 3:13. The paper added a line that said something about the year: his death and five others that weekend brought Wisconsin's 1977 traffic toll to eighty.

David John Nelton had been born in Winona on 19 July 1938, the son of Arthur and Helen (Canfield) Nelton. The 1940 census found the family renting on Lake Park Boulevard in Winona; by 1950 they were in Minnesota City, where his father worked as a carpenter in building construction. He graduated from Winona Senior High, worked for his father the carpenter, and in 1958 married Diane Rivers at Rollingstone.

The couple lived in Minnesota City and then Houston, Minnesota, before crossing the Mississippi to rural Holmen, Wisconsin, about 1971. They had five children. David had become assistant superintendent of maintenance at the La Crosse YMCA.

Wisconsin in those years was a state arguing about how to make its roads safer. The national 55 mph limit had come in at the end of 1973 as an energy measure, and the Wisconsin Department of Transportation credited it in 1974 with a sharp drop in deaths. The research on how much of the fall was due to speed is still disputed, and the paper gave no speeds for David's crash. What the 1977 clipping does show is that eighty families had already lost someone by mid-February.

His funeral was at St. Paul's Catholic Church in Minnesota City, with a Rosary at Fawcett Funeral Home in Winona the night before. The Rev. Joseph C. Frisch officiated; the priest shares the surname of Diane's mother's family, though the paper does not say whether they were related. The ground was frozen, so burial at Oakwood Cemetery, Minnesota City, waited until spring. His pallbearers were Richard Hohensee, Wayne Valentine, Charles Neuman, John Brown, Hollis Donehower and Robert Rolbiecki.

His father, Arthur, had been David's employer before the wedding and now buried his only son; he would live seven more years. Diane was left with five children. Three months later, in May, she married again, a story that belongs to her own chapter.

stories.title: Diane, widowed twice
stories.hook: Between 1975 and 1980 Diane Nelton lost her mother, two husbands and her father, and in the middle of it she took an employer to the state of Wisconsin over her firing.
body: In January 1975 Diane Nelton was out of a job. Her La Crosse employer, E.T.C. Inc., on Division Street, had let her go on the 24th, and a week later, on 31 January, she filed a complaint with the Wisconsin Department of Industry, Labor and Human Relations charging that she had been dismissed because she was a woman. She was thirty-five, a mother of five living in rural Holmen. Title VII of the federal Civil Rights Act of 1964 had made sex discrimination in hiring and firing illegal a decade before, and Wisconsin's Equal Rights Division, set up inside the state government in 1967, was where such complaints went.

She had been born Diane Mary Rivers on 10 August 1939 in St. Paul, the daughter of Edward and Viola (Frisch) Rivers, and grew up at Rollingstone, where her father sold insurance. Her mother had lost her own mother at sixteen months old, and Viola belonged to Holy Trinity all her life and was a charter member of its St. Theresa Society. Viola died in August 1975, while the complaint was still pending.

The case took almost two years. The La Crosse Tribune reported on 17 December 1976 that the hearing examiner had found no evidence that the firing was based on sex and had dismissed the complaint. The ruling came just two months before David, the man she had married at eighteen, was killed on Highway 53, so the loss of the case and the loss of her husband sit in the same winter.

On 28 May 1977, three months after the crash, Diane married Stephen Lee Fascher in La Crosse. He was thirty, from Farmersburg, Iowa, sales manager at La Crosse Glass Co. and a member of the National Guard, and the family settled at Bangor. On Monday 7 August 1978 he died at Lutheran Hospital, the same hospital where David had died; he was thirty-one, and the paper said the cause was unknown pending an autopsy. His obituary lists Diane's five children as his stepchildren, all at home. The two deaths were eighteen months apart.

Her father, Edward, died in January 1980. On 13 August 1983 Diane married Charles Antony in La Crosse and they lived at Bangor. She worked at Hillview Nursing Home until December 1986. Diane M. Antony died of cancer at St. Francis Medical Center on Friday 27 March 1987, at forty-seven, and after a funeral at St. Peter's Catholic Church in Middle Ridge she was buried in St. Mary's Catholic Cemetery at Bangor.

It is a family pattern as much as a personal one. On the Rivers side Viola's father, John Frisch, had been left with three small children when Maggie died in 1906 and had held them together alone. Diane faced the same thing two generations later, with five children, and hers is one of several stories in this family history about the women who carried a household when a husband was gone.

stories.title: Arthur Nelton, carpenter and fireman
stories.hook: Arthur Nelton framed houses around Winona through the Depression and after, sat on the Minnesota City council, fought fires as a volunteer, and outlived his only son.
body: The 1940 census, at a rented house on Lake Park Boulevard in Winona, lists a man of thirty: Arthur Nelton, carpenter, one year of college, earning $1,800 a year. With him were his wife Helen and their small son David. He had earned that wage in a trade that nearly vanished a few years earlier. Homebuilding in the United States fell by about eighty percent between 1929 and 1932, and construction was among the industries the Depression hit hardest.

Arthur R. Nelton had been born in Winona on 27 October 1909, one of four children of George Nelton and Anna Brose, both of German background, and his father was already a house carpenter working his way toward a contracting firm. His mother died in April 1928, when he was eighteen. When George later organized his own firm, his sons Arthur and Irwin joined him in it.

On 15 August 1934, with the building trades still near their lowest point, he married Helen Canfield in Winona. She had been born on 9 November 1910 at Kellogg, in Wabasha County, to James and Nel (Heffernan) Canfield. Her father died at Wabasha on 19 June 1912, when she was nineteen months old. After the wedding she kept house in Minnesota City for most of her life and belonged to St. Paul's Catholic Church there.

By 1950 the census found the family in Minnesota City, with David and a daughter, Sandra. Arthur was a carpenter in building construction, and his obituary calls him a self-employed carpenter in the Winona area until he retired in 1979. He belonged to the Carpenters Union, Local 307, part of a brotherhood that carpenters had founded in 1881, and he served on the Minnesota City council and in the Minnesota City Volunteer Fire Department, the kind of small-town volunteer service where the men who build a village also put out its fires. David worked for him before his marriage.

Helen died at home on 30 November 1982, aged seventy-two, and her grandsons Dirk and Kendrick carried her coffin. Two years later, on 7 October 1984, Arthur died at Lutheran Hospital in La Crosse, the same hospital where his son David had died in 1977. He was seventy-four. Dirk and Kendrick were his pallbearers too. He had spent his working life putting up other families' houses; in the last seven years of his life he buried his only son and then his wife.

quotes.t: He was a member of the Carpenters Union, Local 307, a past member of the Minnesota City Council and a past member of the Minnesota City Volunteer Fire Department.

stories.title: George Nelton built Winona
stories.hook: George Nelton framed Winona houses for four decades, went south to the Florida boom for two winters, and was working until three months before he died.
body: Winona's newspaper gave George Nelton the sort of obituary a builder wants. He "built many of the homes in the city and some of the early stores, and also remodeled some of the Winona store fronts." He had gone on working until 1 August 1952; one of the last houses he finished was the Arthur Tarras home in Glen Mary. Three months later, on 12 November, he died at Winona General Hospital at seventy after a long illness.

He was the first of his family born in America. George John Nelton arrived in Winona on 17 January 1882, the son of German-born George Nelton and Eda Zenk, and he never lived anywhere else. The city he grew up in had been laid out thirty years earlier and built its fortunes on lumber, wheat, steamboats and railroads. German and Polish families had followed the Yankee founders, and by the 1880s there was steady work for anyone who could frame a house or hang a door.

The 1910 census finds him at 617 West King Street, twenty-eight years old, a house carpenter renting with his wife Anna (Brose) and four small children: Myrtle, Irwin, Edward and the baby, Arthur, who was Rachel's great-grandfather. His father, according to the family tree, died the year after, on 19 October 1911; no death record has been seen. George worked as a carpenter, then for the contracting firm of Hanson & Nelton, and finally organized a firm of his own, in which his sons Arthur and Irwin worked.

In the winters of 1924 and 1925 he went to Florida and took contracting work there. Those were the peak years of the Florida land boom, when Northern money and Northern builders poured into Miami and the new planned towns around it, and when the shortage of building supplies grew so bad that the railroads put an embargo on freight in October 1925. Within a year the boom was over, and the 1926 Miami hurricane finished it. The record does not say where in Florida he worked or what he built, only that a Winona contractor went south twice and came home.

Anna died in April 1928, when Arthur was eighteen. In 1930 George married Christine Walstad, a Norwegian immigrant who had come to America in 1904, and the second marriage brought three stepsons, three stepdaughters and nine step-grandchildren into the family; his obituary lists them alongside his own children. He was a member of the Eagles Club and of the Winona Contractors Association, and "an enthusiastic fisherman."

He was buried in Woodlawn Cemetery. One of the men who carried him was named Ernest Brose, the name of Anna's brother, who had spent his own working life in the Northwestern Railway yards. Anna's family, the Broses, is told in the stories that follow.

stories.title: The Rivers family of Rollingstone
stories.hook: Edward Rivers sold insurance in a small Catholic village above the Mississippi; his wife Viola lived there all her married life.
body: Viola M. Frisch was born on 9 June 1905 at Oak Ridge, Minnesota, a daughter of John Frisch. She married Edward Nicholas Rivers at Rollingstone on 14 June 1933 and lived there the rest of her life. Edward was an insurance agent in the village.

Rollingstone was a Catholic farming village in the hills west of Winona, and the Rivers family filled the pews at Holy Trinity. When their daughter Diane married in 1958, the wedding party, the organist, the ushers and the reception helpers were nearly all Rivers relatives, and 350 guests came to the reception on the lawn of the Rivers home.

Viola belonged to Holy Trinity Church, was a charter member of the St. Theresa Society, and was a member of the ladies aid. She died in August 1975, survived by Edward, her daughters Diane Nelton of Holmen and Mary Lynn Dahm of Newport, Rhode Island, a sister, Gertrude Koetter of Minneiska, and eight grandchildren. Msgr. Frank Klein said her funeral Mass at Holy Trinity, and she was buried in the church cemetery.

stories.title: Cleave and Willie Williams, and a horse thief
stories.hook: Melba Bell's parents farmed at Van Alstyne. Her father's youngest brother went to Huntsville prison at seventeen for horse theft.
body: Grover Cleveland "Cleave" Williams was born on 1 June 1887 at Shiloh, Tennessee, the farm country around the old battlefield, the son of Thomas Henry Williams and Rebecca Jane Britton, who moved the family to Texas. Thomas and Rebecca are buried at Van Alstyne; their stone gives 9 February 1847 to 25 December 1933 for him and 14 February 1850 to 20 September 1927 for her.

Willie Parker was born on 13 January 1891 in Texas, the daughter of James and Amanda (Pipkin) Parker. She and Cleave married in Van Alstyne, and their daughter Melba was born there in 1918. Rachel's tree had Cleave and Willie swapped as father and mother; Melba's death certificate and her obituary both name Cleave Williams as her father and Willie Parker as her mother.

Cleave died on 5 December 1949. Willie lived another twenty-five years, a member of the Van Alstyne First Methodist Church, and died in a Sherman hospital on the morning of 18 November 1974, aged eighty-three.

Cleave's youngest brother George, born in 1891 near Mantua, is the subject of a family story written for the Van Alstyne cemetery pages. At seventeen he and a friend, John Leo Skipworth, were arrested for stealing a horse and George went to the state prison at Huntsville. The family legend is that he went calling on a girl, found another man had got there first, took the rival's horse and rode it to death. In prison he developed "sugar diabetes"; he was released and died a few weeks later, on 31 May 1911, with his parents at his bedside. He was twenty.

stories.title: The Canfields of Canfield Springs
stories.hook: A Pennsylvania family were the first settlers of a Minnesota valley in 1855, and a spring still carries their name.
body: In the summer of 1855 Patrick McDonough and John Canfield became the first settlers of Highland township in Wabasha County, Minnesota. The 1884 county history says they "built small homes for themselves, installed their families therein, and went to work." John and his wife Margaret (Greer) were Pennsylvanians who settled where Canfield Springs now is, the first settlers in the upper part of Cook's Valley.

John Canfield was a community man. On 8 November 1857 the neighbours met in G. A. Cook's house to organise a school district and named him director. The first road in the township, laid out in 1858, ran between Appel's Mill and Canfield Springs. The couple farmed there the rest of their lives and raised ten children.

Their son John A. Canfield, born on 29 June 1848, settled at Kellogg and married Anna Hall, the only daughter of George W. Hall, a Pennsylvania-born furniture dealer of Wabasha. Anna's son James Garfield Canfield was born in September 1881, and she died the following February.

James Garfield Canfield married Helen "Nel" Heffernan and lived at Kellogg, where their daughter Helen was born in November 1910. He died at Wabasha on 19 June 1912, aged thirty. Helen, Rachel's great-grandmother, grew up to marry Arthur Nelton in Winona in 1934.

James Garfield Canfield is buried at St. Agnes Cemetery in Kellogg. Find a Grave names his mother as Ann E. Hall Canfield (born 18 August 1855 in Iowa, died 24 February 1882 at Kellogg) and lists his brothers and sisters, among them George (called Duke), John Wilson, Anna Flint, Walter, Homer, Edith, Margaret Bayer, Ruth, Elmer and Beryl Rock, with his daughter Helen as his only child. The cemetery has no Heffernan or other entry that identifies Nel's parents or her later life; her later name is still open.

quotes.t: Patrick McDonough and John Canfield were the first settlers of this town. They came in the summer of 1855 and built small homes for themselves, installed their families therein, and went to work.

stories.title: Boswell and Soper, two railroad towns
stories.hook: The Johnsons and Tysons lived in Choctaw County towns that did not exist before the railway came in 1902.
body: Rachel's Johnson and Tyson families lived for four generations in the southern part of Choctaw County, Oklahoma, in the old Choctaw Nation: George Washington Johnson and Marjorie (Fail) Johnson died at Soper in 1932 and 1926, Joe Johnson was born there in 1908, Opal Tyson was born at Sand Bluff in 1919, and Cornelius Tyson, Joe and Bob Johnson all died at or near Boswell.

Soper is eleven miles west of Hugo on U.S. Highway 70. The Encyclopedia of Oklahoma History says that in 1902 "dwellings and businesses began to spring up" when the Arkansas and Choctaw Railway built through the area. The post office opened in April 1903, and by 1920 the town had 538 people, two banks, four churches and three cotton gins.

Boswell is older than its railroad. About two miles north stood Mayhew, where Choctaws settled after removal; Presbyterians opened a mission school there in 1839, and it became the court ground of the Choctaw Nation's Pushmataha District. When the railway came through in 1902 the businesses moved south to the tracks, and the post office was renamed for Amity V. Boswell, who surveyed the right-of-way.
The Boswell News and the Soper Democrat carried the towns' news for decades. A tornado destroyed most of Soper's brick downtown in 1960.

stories.title: Is the Johnson line related to a Vice President?
stories.hook: Rachel's tree runs the Johnsons back to Great Crossing, Kentucky, and the family of Vice President Richard M. Johnson. No record yet proves the key link.
body: Col. Robert Johnson (1745–1815) and Jemima Suggett of Great Crossing, Scott County, Kentucky, had eleven children. One was Richard Mentor Johnson, Vice President of the United States from 1837 to 1841. Another was Joel Johnson (1790–1846), who married Verlinda Offutt in 1817, founded Lakeport Plantation on Lake Chicot in Arkansas about 1831, and is buried in Frankfort Cemetery beside his brother Richard.

Rachel's tree makes Joel the grandfather of George Washington Johnson, who was born in Mississippi in 1851 and died at Soper, Oklahoma, in 1932, through a son called Jonathan T. Johnson (1824–1859). The geography is possible, since Chicot County and the Mississippi Delta are neighbours.

But no source names a Jonathan among Joel's children; the Lakeport records list Lycurgus, Julia, Betsy and Cyrus. Joel had a brother called John Telemachus Johnson (1788–1856), and the name may have been garbled in a copied tree. Until a record ties George Washington Johnson to Kentucky, this is a family lead, not a fact. The Scottish noble ancestry further up the same branch (the Earls of Annandale) is a well-known copied-tree error.

stories.title: Rollingstone: a Luxembourg village on the Rolling Stone creek
stories.hook: A creek the Dakota named for a rolling stone, a utopian colony that failed, and the Luxembourg farmers who stayed and built the stone church where Diane Rivers married.
body: Rollingstone sits where the north and west valleys of the Rolling Stone creek meet, a few miles up from the Mississippi in Winona County. The name is older than the village. The 1883 county history records the Dakota name for the creek, and Wikipedia gives the translation as 'the stream where the stone rolls'. White settlement began in 1852, when the Western Farm and Village Association, an idealistic colony organized in New York, laid out a town of large lots at the creek mouth. The history says the association chose the table lands near the mouth of the creek 'for the village, naming the village Minnesota City and the township Rolling Stone.' The colony struggled, but the township name stayed.

The village that bears the name today is a different settlement, farther up the valley, and it was founded by people from Luxembourg. The National Register nomination for Holy Trinity Church dates the first arrivals to 1855: 'the first German settlers from Luxembourg arrived in the rolling hills of Winona County.' The Rivers family is a clear case. The 1913 county history says Michael and Margaret (Adam) Rivers 'came to America in 1854, and settled on a farm in Winona county in 1855,' and their son John B. Rivers was 'brought to Winona county in 1855 and lived with his parents in Rollingstone township.' The Frisch family came later, in July 1864 or 1865, and settled on nearby Oak Ridge, where the 1883 history notes the Catholic church was begun at a meeting at John Speltz's house on 5 December 1875 and that 'the majority of the settlers are steady, frugal Luxemburgers.'

The 1883 history describes the village in a few lines: 'The inhabitants of the village and of the vicinity are Germans. It contains three stores, two hotels, two blacksmith shops, a fine stone church and neat parsonage, a schoolhouse and two or three saloons. The church belongs to the Catholic denomination, and nearly all the people in the vicinity are members.' Luxembourg was then part of the German Confederation's cultural world, which is why the clerk wrote 'Germans' for people who called themselves Luxembourgers. The same book puts the stone church at the center of everything, with a Catholic burial ground beside it.

Holy Trinity Church was built in 1869 under Charles Wender, of rough-cut limestone, 35 by 60 feet, in Gothic Revival style with lancet windows. The nomination says the parishioners 'provided the labor and financial aid' both then and in 1893, when a transept and chancel designed to double the seating were added under the local carpenter Nicholas Arnoldy. A cemetery and a first frame church were already in place by 1861. A grade school followed in 1886 and a new school and the community's first high school in 1921; Edward N. Rivers is recorded as a Holy Trinity High School graduate. The church was listed on the National Register in 1984 as the 'pivotal element in the Rollingstone community.'

For the families in this tree the church marks every turning point. John Frisch's funeral in 1934, Viola Frisch Rivers's in 1975 and Edward N. Rivers's in 1980 were all held at Holy Trinity, and all three were buried in Rollingstone or Oak Ridge cemeteries. Diane Rivers and David Nelton were married there in 1958. Village life ran on Luxembourg-style parish societies: Edward Rivers Sr. and his son Edward both belonged to the St. Nicholas Society, and Edward Jr. served sixteen years as its president, while Viola was a charter member of the St. Theresa Society. The village also sustained its own Rollingstone Mutual Fire Insurance company, whose secretary for 24 years was John Frisch and on whose board Edward N. Rivers later sat. The local historian Mary E. Nilles wrote the standard account, Rollingstone: A Luxembourgish Village in Minnesota (1983), which the National Register nomination cites.

quotes.t: In 1855, the first German settlers from Luxembourg arrived in the rolling hills of Winona County. Bringing with them their strong Catholic religious heritage, the immigrants had, by 1861, established a cemetery and built a church.

stories.title: The Rivers family: from Heffingen to the Rollingstone post office
stories.hook: Michel Rivers brought nine children from Luxembourg in 1854; his sons ran the Rollingstone post office for decades, and his grandson Edward carried its mail.
body: The Rivers name at Rollingstone traces to Michel Rivers (1804-1880) and Margaretha Adehm (1807-1884), who left Luxembourg in 1854. Their son Henry was born at Heffingen, in the canton of Mersch, on 11 April 1838, according to the Find a Grave transcription of his memorial. The 1913 county history confirms the move without naming the village: Michael and Margaret (Adam) Rivers 'came to America in 1854, and settled on a farm in Winona county in 1855.' No document seen explains how the spelling Rivers relates to a Luxembourg original, so a link to a name such as Rieffers remains unchecked. The Rivers name is already Rivers in every American record found.

John Baptiste Rivers, born in Luxembourg on 16 June 1840, made the family's public name. He enlisted in March 1865 in Co. K of the 48th Wisconsin Volunteer Infantry and served at Fort Lyon, Colorado, 'protecting the frontier against the Indians.' After the war he farmed in Norton township, then in 1872 opened a store in Rollingstone village. He was postmaster for 27 years, first president of the village council, and a founder of the First State Bank of Rollingstone. The post office history reads: 'In 1886, J. B. Rivers succeeded Hy. Rivers.' Henry Rivers, his brother, had held the office and died on 10 June 1886, the year the change was made.

Henry's wife Elizabeth Lehnertz was born in Luxembourg in 1847 and came over in 1860. Their sons were Henry, who died in 1929, and Edward, born in Rollingstone on 4 November 1881. After Henry's death in 1886 the family ran a hotel in the village. Edward Sr. went to the parochial school, became the rural mail carrier on the route that opened in February 1903, and kept at it for 30 years, retiring on 1 March 1934. He also helped found the Rollingstone Co-operative Oil Association, sold insurance for Farmers Home Mutual, and served as mayor from 1938 to 1948. On 22 June 1909 he married Johanna Johns, and nine children followed, the first of them Edward Nicholas on 20 October 1910.

Edward N. Rivers went into insurance at Rollingstone in 1934, the year after he married Viola Frisch. His own obituary lists a graduate of Holy Trinity High School, a director of the Rollingstone Mutual Fire Insurance Co., president of the Rollingstone Business Association and the St. Nicholas Society, a Knight of Columbus and an Elk. It records his two marriages and that he died at home on 14 January 1980 'after an illness of several months.' It names no military service. His brother Francis, born 1927, had died on 22 November 1944, aged 17; the obituary says only 'a son Francis died November 22, 1944.' The brothers Bernard, Norbert, Arthur and Paul carried Edward to the grave.

The Rivers and Frisch families were already intertwined before Edward and Viola married. Viola's aunt Katherine Frisch had married Matthew Rivers, John B.'s son and Edward's first cousin once removed, on 19 November 1907, and the couple ran a grocery in Rollingstone. John Frisch's 1934 obituary lists 'Mrs. Mathew Rivers, Rollingstone' among his sisters.

stories.title: Oak Ridge, autumn 1906: two funerals in three weeks
stories.hook: Viola Frisch was sixteen months old when her mother died, and nineteen days later her grandfather, the Luxembourg pioneer, followed.
body: Jacques Frisch was born at Beaufort in the canton of Echternach on 28 October 1837, and Anna Speltz was born at Fischbach in the canton of Mersch on 24 October 1836, according to Find a Grave transcriptions. Anna's obituary says: 'Miss Anna Speltz was born in Luxembourg on October 24, 1836. She was married in Luxembourg to Jacques Frisch, and together they came to this country in 1864, and landed at Winona on July 4 in that year, and settled in Oak Ridge.' Jacques's own obituary dates the arrival to 4 July 1865, so one of the two papers is a year off. Find a Grave lists several Speltz siblings for Anna, among them Nicholas, Mathew, Peter, Theodore and John. The 1883 county history says the Oak Ridge Catholic congregation was organized at a meeting at the house of John Speltz on 5 December 1875, and Jacob Frisch is named in the 1883 county history among the men whose efforts built it.

Anna died on 7 May 1902 at Oak Ridge after nearly a year's illness, 'one of the pioneer women of this country.' Their son John P. Frisch, born 25 July 1873, taught school for eight years and on 1 October 1901 married Margaret 'Maggie' Haines of Arcadia, Wisconsin. Three children came: Gertrude in 1903, Viola on 9 June 1905, and a third child in the fall of 1906 (the 1934 obituary names a son Raymond among the survivors).

On the evening of 1 October 1906, Maggie died at home at about eight o'clock. The Winona Republican-Herald of 2 October reported: 'Mr. and Mrs. Frisch were married five years ago yesterday. She is survived by her husband and three children, the youngest being fourteen days of age.' She was 31. The funeral was held at the Oak Ridge Catholic Church that Thursday. Nineteen days later, on Saturday 20 October, her father-in-law Jacob Frisch died of diabetes at the age of 69. His obituary calls him 'one of the old settlers and highly esteemed citizens of Winona county' and names 'John, whose wife died two weeks ago' among his survivors.

John Frisch kept the family together. He farmed the old Frisch homestead on Oak Ridge until about 1929, then moved to Rollingstone, where he became secretary of the Rollingstone Mutual Farmers Fire Insurance Company for 24 years and, in 1932, president of the state association of mutual insurance companies. He remarried in 1931 to Mrs. Anna Breitbach of Winona. His daughter Viola married Edward Rivers in June 1933, and John died the next March, on 16 March 1934, of an acute heart attack, 'while members of his family were at his bedside.' Edward N. Rivers began as an insurance agent at Rollingstone the same year.

stories.title: From Mantua to the Railroad Towns
stories.hook: A seminary town that died when the railroad missed it, and the two towns that grew in its place.
body: Mantua was founded in 1854 to pay for a school. William C. McKinney, James W. Throckmorton and Joseph Wilcox bought 200 acres from a son of Collin McKinney, divided it into lots and sold them to fund Mantua Seminary. The town banned gambling, horse racing and the sale of liquor to keep a proper environment for the students. By 1860 it had three stores, a church and about fifty people, and by 1870 about 300.

Then the Houston and Texas Central Railway laid its tracks two miles east in 1872. Some Mantua citizens bought land by the line and started a new town, Van Alstyne, in Grayson County. By mid-1873 Mantua was deserted except for the churches, which moved in 1888. The post office closed on 11 July 1873. Van Alstyne incorporated in 1890 with about 400 people, two gristmills, a flour mill, a newspaper and a college, and had about 1,940 residents around 1900.

Anna, five miles southeast of old Mantua, came a little later. The same railroad passed through in 1873, and the town was platted in 1883 with twenty people, two stores, a steam gristmill and a Baptist church. It had 100 to 200 people by 1890, incorporated in 1913, and had its first bank in 1902. Its population was 538 in 1929 and 467 in 1931. The Greenville and Northwestern Railway, a traction line from Anna to Blue Ridge, opened about 1915 and was abandoned in 1920.

The country around them was farm country. Collin County had 903 farms in 1870 and 6,001 in 1920, when it grew 49,311 bales of cotton, 2,574,689 bushels of corn and 956,412 bushels of wheat. Grayson County's farms peaked at 5,762 in 1900, the year of its largest corn crop. Roads were paved or graveled from the 1910s and 1920s. In the Depression, farms in Collin County fell from 6,069 in 1930 to 4,771 in 1940, and Grayson County's from 5,169 to 4,296.

Rachel's families fit this map. A Williams son was born at Mantua in 1891, the Parkers' death places in the tree are Monta and Van Alstyne, and Wayne Douglas Bell was born at Anna in 1914 and later farmed in Grayson County. The Williams and Parker graves are at Van Alstyne. Each of these families lived within a few miles of the abandoned Mantua town site.

stories.title: The Fails move from Jasper County, Mississippi, to Milam County, Texas
stories.hook: Rayford Fail's household was in Milam County by the 1870 census, and some of his grandchildren later turned up in the Choctaw Nation too.
body: Rayford Fail was born on 16 March 1806, probably in Johnston County, North Carolina, and married Polly Anne Wallace by 1838. Their children were born in Jasper County, Mississippi: George Washington in August 1847, Young Rayford in December 1853, Jeremiah Marsh in March 1854, Thomas in February 1857 and Temperence Elizabeth in February 1863. Marjorie Rebecca, the daughter Rachel's tree places at Turnersville, Jasper County, in 1849, fits neatly into that run of Jasper County births, although the published family trees seen so far do not list her among Rayford's children.

The move west came during or just after the Civil War. The 1870 census enumerates "Raford Failes," sixty, born in North Carolina, as head of a household in Milam County, Texas (page 212, line 19), and in the same household his seven-year-old daughter "Elizabeth Failes," born in Mississippi. Because Temperence was born in Mississippi in 1863 and the family was in Texas by mid-1870, the move happened in those seven years. Rayford died in Milam County on 26 January 1885 and his Find a Grave memorial gives his birth as 16 March 1806.

His children made Milam County their own. George Washington Fail married Margaret Ann Johnson in 1870 and died in Milam County in 1923. Young Rayford married Viney Allison in 1873, had three sons, and died in Milam County on 6 September 1880. Temperence, called Lizzie, married Joseph Franklin Keen in Lee County, Texas, on 7 March 1878.

The Keens went on to Lamar County, Texas, and then, shortly after the 1900 census, into the Choctaw Nation. In 1910 "Lizzie Keen," fifty-nine, a widow and head of household, was enumerated at Oakes, Choctaw County, Oklahoma, the same township where Joel Anderson Johnson and Winnie were living that year. Her obituary appeared in The Southeast Oklahoman of Hugo on 14 December 1939, and she was buried at Forest Chapel Cemetery in Lamar County, Texas. Other Fail descendants, among them Thomas Fail (died 1936) and a grandson known as Jim "Tobe" Fail (died 1957), ended up in Choctaw County or Greer County, Oklahoma. The Fails and the Johnsons were not strangers in Choctaw County, whatever the exact tie.

What is not yet proven is the link between this family and Joel Anderson Johnson, born in Milam County in April 1875. His census returns give a father born in Arkansas and a mother born in Mississippi, which is consistent with a Mississippi-born Fail mother, but no record seen so far names her. Rayford's son George Washington Fail also married a Margaret Ann Johnson in Milam County in 1870, and the tree entry for "George Washington Johnson" may have mixed the two George Washingtons together. The 1880 census for Milam County, the Milam County marriage and probate books, and the 1961 obituary's sibling list (Carl, Arthur, Penny Cole, Nannie Harrison and Sally Smith) are the records that would settle it.

stories.title: Anna Brose Nelton and twenty-one years of illness
stories.hook: A Winona contractor's wife died in 1928 after an illness her husband traced to a rattlesnake bite across the lake.
body: Anna Louise Brose was born in Winona on 26 December 1883, the daughter of Ernest and Augusta Brose, and, in the words of her obituary, "spent all her life here." She married the carpenter George J. Nelton, and by 1910 they had four children: Myrtle, Irwin, Edward and Arthur.

The Winona Republican-Herald reported her death under the headline "Mrs. Nelton Dies After Long Illness." She died at 7:15 on a Sunday evening at the family home, 836 West Broadway, "after an illness of 21 years." The paper added a detail that makes the length of that illness specific: her husband "traces his wife's illness to a rattlesnake bite received in June 1907 across the lake." Counting back twenty-one years from 1928 lands on that same summer, when her youngest child, Arthur, was not yet born. He arrived in October 1909.

She left her husband, the four children (Myrtle still unmarried at home), two brothers, Ernest and John Brose, and three sisters, Minnie Brose, Mrs. Max Schulze and Mrs. Niels Skow. The funeral was held at the house and then at McKinley Methodist Church, with burial at Woodlawn Cemetery. Arthur was eighteen.

A note on the date: the transcription on Find a Grave heads the notice "Monday, November 9, 1928," but Anna's death is recorded on 8 April 1928, which was a Sunday, and the obituary says she died on a Sunday. The newspaper issue was almost certainly Monday 9 April, and the month in the transcription is a slip.

stories.title: Ernest and Augusta Brose and their six Winona children
stories.hook: Two Germans who raised their family in Winona, a railroad yardmaster, a wartime veteran and a lot at Woodlawn.
body: Ernest Brose was born in May 1847 and Augusta in December 1856 (the tree gives 1855), both in Germany according to their Find a Grave memorials; the family tree places them in the village of Wolwark, near Schubin in the Bromberg district of Posen. Their first daughter, Anna, was born in Winona in December 1883, so they had crossed the Atlantic and reached Minnesota before that. No passenger list or naturalization record turned up in the free sources.

They had six children who lived to be grown, all born in Winona: Anna (1883), Ida (1885), Louise (born 8 December 1886), Ernest Gustav (born 23 December 1890), Minnie (27 June 1893) and John H. (1 July 1895). Augusta died on 28 April 1924, aged sixty-seven. Ernest lived ten more years and died in Winona on 4 September 1934, aged eighty-seven. Both are buried at Woodlawn Cemetery, Section AA, Lot 66, where their son John also lies.

The children's obituaries sketch Winona lives. Ida married Niels Petersen Skow in 1922 and died in 1946. Louise married Max E. Schulze on 2 January 1911; the Winona Daily News said she "was born to Ernest and Augusta Brose and lived in Winona most of her life." Ernest Gustav became a yardmaster for the Northwestern Railway, retired in September 1948, and in 1949 married Lydia Zambrocki at St. Casimir's Church; as a veteran of the First World War he died at the Minneapolis Veterans Hospital on 1 June 1965 and was buried at St. Mary's Cemetery. Minnie married William Julius Schellhas and died in 1971 in Winona, the last of the six.

The family's churches varied: Anna's funeral was at McKinley Methodist Church and Louise's at Grace Presbyterian, while Ernest Gustav's was at the Catholic St. Casimir's. One more name appears on the Find a Grave family list, a Margaret Caroline Brose (1910), whom Louise's obituary lists among siblings who died before her. Anna's 1928 obituary names five living siblings and no Margaret, and a woman born to a 53-year-old mother in 1910 is unlikely, so that entry is treated as a mix-up and left out of the family above.

stories.title: Eda Zenk Nelton and her six children
stories.hook: A German-born widow who outlived her husband by thirty-two years and lived to ninety-one.
body: Eda Ida Zenk was born in Germany on 15 March 1852 (the tree gives Pommern, a village on the Mosel in the Rhineland) and died in Winona on 30 December 1943, aged ninety-one. Her obituary ran in the Winona Republican-Herald of 31 December 1943, page 3. She is buried at Woodlawn Cemetery. Her husband, George Nelton, born in January 1855, died on 19 October 1911 according to the tree; no obituary for him turned up.

Find a Grave lists six children for her, all born in Winona: Anna (1879, later Mrs. Joseph Knopp, married 1899, died 1974); George John (17 January 1882, the Winona contractor); Winifred, called Winnie (4 March 1882, Mrs. Arthur Oscar Beeman, died 1966); Edith Thelma (17 September 1888, Mrs. Eaton, died at La Crosse in 1962); Harry (1892 to 1966); and Elsie (29 January 1896, Mrs. Victor Z. Bitu, died 1968). Elsie's eldest son, Jenus Arvid Bitu, died in 1927 at thirteen. Two of the dates cannot both be right: George and Winnie are both listed as born in 1882 only seven weeks apart, so one date is wrong or they were not both Eda's.

George John Nelton's second wife was Christine Walstad, born in Norway on 3 December 1888, who came to America in 1904 and married him in 1930. Her obituary in 1958 says she worked at the Williams Hotel Cafeteria, Winona Cleaning Works and Miller Waste Mills, and became a United States citizen in September 1941. It names his surviving children as sons Irwin, Arthur and Edward and daughter Mrs. Andrew (Myrtle) Wally.

A Mrs. Charles Nelton of Winona was badly hurt in January 1913 when her horse bolted in front of a Chicago Great Western train. A Charles Nelton (1 January 1880 to 12 October 1963) lived in Winona with his wife Rose Edith Pearl Nelton; his Find a Grave page lists no parents, and he is not among Eda's children on Find a Grave, so no connection to George's family is shown.

stories.title: Jacob Johns of Hart Township: from Baltimore to Fort Blakely
stories.hook: The father of Johanna Johns Rivers brought twelve children into a Winona County farm after fighting in the Dakota War and the Civil War.
body: Johanna Johns, who married Edward Rivers Sr. of Rollingstone on 22 June 1909, was born on 11 November 1888 at Rushford in Fillmore County, "to Jacob and Theresa Johns," as her obituary in the Winona Daily News on 5 March 1967 says. She died at home in Rollingstone on 4 March 1967 and was buried at Holy Trinity Catholic Cemetery. A brother, George, lived in Canada and a sister, Mrs. Rose Tiernan, in Albertville.

A 1895 biographical album of Winona County gives a Jacob Johns of Hart Township, next to the county line, who matches those names. He was born in Germany on 5 August 1842 and was brought as a three-year-old to America on a voyage of two months, landing at Baltimore. The family spent seven years in Missouri, then went to Hazel Green, Wisconsin, and in 1856 settled in Hart Township.

On 15 August 1862 he enlisted as a private in Company E, Sixth Minnesota Infantry. "His first engagement was at Birch Coolie, September 2, 1862," and the second at Wood Lake on 23 September, then he went south in 1864 to Helena, Arkansas, and the sieges of Spanish Fort and Fort Blakely. He "was never wounded nor taken prisoner" and was discharged on 19 August 1865. He bought eighty acres in section 28, which grew to 440.

On 18 May 1868 he married Theresa (printed "Kryzer" in the book). The twelve children are named as Mary, Sophia, Lizzie, Emma, Annie, Jacob, Henry, Rose, Willie, Hannah, Eddie and George. Johanna's obituary names a sister Rose and a brother George, and Hannah is the likely form of her name, but the book does not list a Johanna, so the match rests on the parents' names, the sibling names and the location. The family was Catholic, Jacob was a Democrat and served as township supervisor and constable, and he belonged to the Grand Army of the Republic.

stories.title: Wings in August, a parade in January
stories.hook: Two hometown newspaper items follow Bob Johnson from jump school in 1958 to the Kennedy inaugural parade in 1961.
body: On Sunday, 31 August 1958, the Hugo Daily News printed a short item on its front page under the headline "Boswell GI Gets Paratroop Wings." It began at Fort Bragg, North Carolina: Pvt. Bobby J. Johnson, son of Joel G. Johnson of the Boehler Route, Boswell, "recently was graduated from the 82d Airborne Division Jump School." He had earned his parachutist wings after a course that included five training jumps.

The item sketches a short Army career so far. Bob was twenty-one. He had entered the Army that February and finished basic training at Fort Ord, California, and before that he had attended Decatur Baptist College in Texas. The mother named is Mrs. Nettie B. McCarter of Route 2, Sherman, Texas. His father was still on the Boehler Route, the farm road outside Boswell where Joe Johnson would live until he died in 1972.

Jump school at Fort Bragg was the gate to the Army's airborne divisions. The 82nd Airborne, headquartered there, was a Strategic Army Corps unit, which the Army described as ready to deploy anywhere on short notice.

Less than three years later the Durant Daily Democrat of 29 January 1961 ran a photograph and a longer piece headed "Boswell Boy Was In Inauguration Parade." Specialist Four Bobby J. Johnson had marched with the 82nd Airborne's 504th Infantry in the parade for President John F. Kennedy in Washington. He was a supply clerk in the Mortar Battery, based at Fort Bragg, and "last stationed in Germany." The paper said he was twenty-three and a 1957 graduate of Decatur, Texas, High School. His obituary, written sixty-three years later, says Savoy, the town where his mother later lived.

His mother's name changed in the three years between the items. In 1958 she is Mrs. Nettie B. McCarter of Route 2, Sherman; in 1961, Mrs. Nettie B. Tillery of Sadler, Texas. She had been Nettie Tyson, and the household she grew up in is told in the story of the two Tyson sisters. She died on 6 February 1980 and is buried at Sunnyside Cemetery in Savoy, Fannin County, Texas, her last residence.

These were the Army's own hometown releases, mailed from Fort Bragg to the papers in a soldier's home county. They are the earliest published record of a career that would run twenty years through Germany, Korea and Vietnam and end with a Warrant Officer 3's rank. Eleven months after the parade, on 21 December 1961, he married Margie Bell.

stories.title: A license in July 1938
stories.hook: The Choctaw County court docket records Opal Tyson's marriage license, the first step toward the Wilson, Johnson and Tyson household of 1940.
body: In the Paris News of 12 July 1938, under the heading "Choctaw County, Hugo, Okla., 17th Judicial District, George R. Childers, Judge," the court report listed new cases filed: a shoe company against a debtor, two divorces, another divorce. Then came a short list headed "Marriage Licenses Issued." Its first line reads: "Seidel Wilson to Opal Tyson, Boswell."

The Southeast Oklahoman of Hugo repeated the list nine days later, on 21 July 1938, spelling the groom's name "Seidel Wilson and Opal Tyson, of Boswell." Opal was eighteen. In the 1940 census she is back at her father Albert Tyson's rented farm at Oakes as "Opal Wilson," twenty-one, with a three-month-old son, in the same house as her sister Nettie Johnson and Nettie's boy Bobbin.

The two sisters had thus married within a few years of each other, one to Joe Johnson and one to a Wilson. Opal's later marriage to Joe Johnson, recorded in Sevier County, Arkansas, in 1968, is told in the story of the two Tyson sisters; this item is the paper record that places her first marriage in July 1938.
